subject: Climate & Environment
title: Ocean Acidification
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Ocean Acidification.

hook.text: The ocean absorbs about 30% of human CO₂. That sounds helpful — until it isn't.

buildup.text: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, slowly lowering the pH of seawater worldwide.

discovery.text: Ocean acidity has jumped 30% since the Industrial Revolution began.

twist.text: Acidic water dissolves shells of corals and plankton at the base of the food chain.

climax.text: If plankton collapse, the entire marine food web could unravel with them.

punchline.text: The ocean is paying the bill for our carbon habit.

quiz.question: How much has ocean acidity increased since the Industrial Revolution?

details.summary: The ocean has absorbed roughly 30 percent of human CO2 emissions, which react with seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering ocean pH by 0.1 units since pre-industrial times. This 26 percent increase in acidity threatens shellfish, corals, and the entire marine food chain.
details.whyItMatters: Acidification is climate change's equally dangerous twin. It undermines marine ecosystems that billions depend on for food, even before warming-related damage begins.
takeaways: Ocean pH has dropped 0.1 units, a 26 percent acidity increase
Acidification makes it harder for shellfish and corals to build shells
Pteropods, tiny sea snails at the base of food chains, dissolve in acidic water

faq.question: Why does a 0.1 pH change matter?
faq.answer: The pH scale is logarithmic, so a 0.1 drop represents a 26 percent increase in hydrogen ion concentration. Marine organisms evolved in remarkably stable conditions, and even small changes impair shell formation, reproduction, and behavior.

faq.question: Can marine life adapt to more acidic water?
faq.answer: Some species show limited adaptation over generations, but the current rate of pH change is 100 times faster than any in the past 300 million years. Most organisms cannot evolve fast enough, and ecosystem interactions compound individual species' vulnerability.
